[Curiosity (care) killed the cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_killed_the_cat) was originally quoted by a famous playwright in 1589

[Curiosity killed the cat, but satisfaction brought it back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_killed_the_cat,_but_satisfaction_brought_it_back) wasn't published until 1905

[Blood is thicker that water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_killed_the_cat,_but_satisfaction_brought_it_back) can be traced back to 1180 while the covenant phrase can only be traced back to 1893

[Jack of all trades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_of_all_trades,_master_of_none) is a little harder to nail down because it has changed a number of times based on who was using it.  First just 'Jack of all trade', then the 'master of none' as added, finally the 'still better than the master of one' was added.

[Great minds think alike](https://english.stackexchange.com/questions/295406/what-is-the-origin-of-the-phrase-great-minds-think-alike) can be traced to "Good wits doe jumpe" but the second part appears to have been added later.

So, once again, researching something on the internet shows that something on the internet is wrong.
Great minds is harder to nail down because the oldest version found seems to be "Good wits doe jumpe". Again it appears the second part was added later as it is harder to find where it came from.
